gitApps.name: browser-connector
gitApps.description: Attach your own everyday browser to a PersonalClaw you already run. A browse task with target 'user_browser' can then act inside a session you are already logged into, and only in a tab it opens for itself: when you allow a task, the extension opens a new background tab in a tab group named after the task (or a window of its own, in a browser without tab groups), and the run never touches a tab you already have open. Close the group to stop the run; bring its tab to the front to take over, which pauses it. If the extension cannot open a tab of the run's own, the task is refused. The extension pairs with the gateway the way your phone does and talks to it over loopback only: its host permissions are loopback-only, and it opens no listening surface of its own. In your browser it asks for tabs (to open the run's tab and act on it), tab groups (to name the run's group and notice when you close it) and storage (its settings, and which tab belongs to which run). It speaks a narrow, closed contract: navigate, read-outline, click, type, close. It never reads, stores, or types into a password field.

gitApps.name: ops
gitApps.description: An on-call first responder that walks the shift with you. It files each alarm your monitor writes as an incident, ranks the queue by what needs a human first, and works each one with you — claim, investigate against your own runbook, record findings, propose a fix. Proposing changes nothing, and running a fix is off by default, needs an explicit confirm, and can only ever be a command your own runbook already declared.
gitApps.author: PersonalClaw

crons.name: ops-sweep
crons.message:
Take one on-call sweep.

1. Call ops_watch. If it opened and reopened nothing, stop — say nothing and end the turn.
2. For each incident it opened or reopened at severity high or critical, or that paged: ops_claim it, then ops_investigate to get its plan.
3. Walk that plan with your own READ-ONLY tools. Call ops_record once per check with what you actually saw, including the ones that came back clean — a ruled-out cause is worth as much to the next responder as a found one.
4. When you can name a fix, call ops_propose_fix with the fix, its blast radius and its rollback. If the incident's runbook declares an action that is the fix, name it.
5. NEVER call ops_apply_fix. An unattended turn does not get to change the system — leave the proposal and its confirm token for a human.

If you cannot name a fix, record why not and leave the incident claimed. An honest 'not diagnosed, here is what was ruled out' is the useful outcome.

launches.why: Applying a fix runs the command a runbook action of yours declares, exactly as your runbook gives it.

gitApps.name: research-lab
gitApps.description: Unattended research campaigns as an agent tool. One question becomes a tree of sub-questions that hourly cycles work down through subagents, recording findings with their sources. When the tree is answered — or the cycle budget runs out — it synthesizes everything into one markdown report on your machine.
gitApps.author: PersonalClaw

crons.name: advance-campaigns
crons.message:
Advance the open Research Lab campaign by one cycle.

1. Call research_next. If its metadata says done: true, call research_report once and stop — do not open a new campaign.
2. Otherwise take the worklist it returns and research each sub-question in its own subagent, in parallel, so one slow question does not stall the cycle.
3. For each answered sub-question call research_record with the finding, the sources it rests on, and any follow-up questions the work raised.
4. Stop after this one cycle. The next cron tick runs the next one.

Record what you actually found, including "no reliable source says" — an unattended campaign is only worth reading if its findings are honest.
